opus-5.5.text:
Failure is the normal state of affairs. If you look at how we actually built AlphaFold, the vast majority of ideas we tried didn't work. Most of them didn't even fail interestingly. They just failed. So the question isn't how to avoid failure. It's how to fail cheaply, quickly, and informatively.

A few things matter a lot to me.

**Make experiments fast.** If an idea takes three weeks to test, you get maybe fifteen shots a year, and you'll treat each one with a kind of reverence that makes you bad at letting go. If you can get a meaningful signal in a day, or even a few hours on a smaller version of the problem, you can afford to be wrong constantly. Much of the real engineering work is building the infrastructure and the proxy tasks that let you be wrong cheaply.

**Distinguish "the idea is bad" from "the implementation is bad."** In machine learning, a good idea with a bug looks almost exactly like a bad idea. The network still trains, the loss still goes down, you just get a slightly worse number. So when something fails, ask whether you've actually tested the hypothesis or just tested your code. Sometimes the most valuable thing is going back to an idea the team dismissed six months earlier and discovering it was killed by a normalization bug.

**Don't over-read single results.** There's a lot of noise. Seeds matter, and small differences can be meaningless. I've seen people build an elaborate story around a 0.3% improvement that disappears on the next run. Part of a healthy relationship with failure is a healthy skepticism toward success.

**Failures accumulate into understanding.** Even when individual experiments don't pan out, a hundred negative results tell you something about the shape of the problem: where the difficulty actually lives, which inductive biases matter, what the model is and isn't learning. With protein structure, many of our failures pointed toward needing the network to reason much more directly about geometry and about the relationships between residues. That wasn't one experiment telling us that. It was the pattern across many of them.

**Culturally, people have to feel safe saying "this didn't work."** If a team rewards only wins, people quietly stop running risky experiments, or they spend weeks tuning a dead idea because they don't want to report it as dead. The most productive environments I've been in treat a clean negative result as a real contribution, because it is one. It saves everybody else from going down that path.

So I'd say failure is the raw material. The skill is in designing your process so you get through it efficiently and actually learn from it, rather than just enduring it.

r001.rationale: The response says the “vast majority” of ideas tried for AlphaFold did not work, showing that many failures can accompany a successful project. It does not clearly state that roughly nine out of ten experiments fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, failure is most of what we do. When I look back at AlphaFold, the vast majority of ideas we tried didn't work, and I think that's the normal state of research rather than something to be embarrassed about. The question isn't whether you fail, it's how cheaply and how informatively you fail.

So the way I think about it is in terms of iteration speed. If an experiment takes a week to tell you something, you get maybe fifty shots a year. If it takes an hour, you get thousands. A lot of our effort went into making the loop fast, so that being wrong was inexpensive. That changes your psychology too. You stop being precious about ideas because you're not investing much in any one of them.

The other thing is that a failed experiment should still teach you something about the problem. If you try something and it doesn't help, that's a data point about what the model actually needs. We spent a lot of time looking at where the predictions were wrong, not just the aggregate metric, and often the failures told us more than the successes. Occasionally you'd see a case where the model clearly had the right physics in mind but couldn't express it, and that pointed to an architectural change rather than more data or more training.

I'd also say you have to be careful to distinguish between an idea failing and your implementation of it failing. A lot of good ideas get abandoned because the first version had a bug, or the hyperparameters were off, and nobody went back. So there's some judgment in deciding when to push harder on something versus when to let it go. Usually my heuristic is that if the reason it should work is sound, give it a few serious attempts before you write it off.

And then there's the larger scale failure, which is spending years on an approach that turns out to be the wrong one. That's harder to protect against. The best defense I know of is being honest with yourself about whether progress is real or whether you're just fitting your intuitions to the noise. We had periods on AlphaFold where things plateaued and it wasn't obvious whether we were close or fundamentally stuck. You have to keep asking whether the thing you're doing is still the most promising path, and be willing to tear up a lot of work when the answer is no.

r001.rationale: The response says the “vast majority” of AlphaFold ideas did not work and frames that as normal, but it does not communicate the specific roughly nine-out-of-ten proportion.

astra-6.text:
I try to think about failure in terms of what you’ve learned. You have an idea, you run an experiment, and it doesn’t work. But that can mean several different things. The idea might be wrong, the implementation might be wrong, or the experiment might not actually test the thing you thought it tested.

The useful question is: what do I believe now that I didn’t believe before? If the answer is nothing, then perhaps you need a better experiment. A negative result that really rules something out can be incredibly valuable.

The hard part is balancing persistence with being willing to change your mind. You need to give an idea a fair chance without making its success a condition of your own success. You’re trying to understand the problem, and sometimes the best progress is discovering why your favorite approach won’t solve it.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses learning from failed experiments and persistence, but does not state that being wrong in roughly nine out of ten experiments is compatible with research success.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important thing is to make failure informative. You have some idea about why a change should help, you run the experiment, and it doesn’t. The temptation is to say, “Well, that didn’t work,” and move on. But did it fail in the way you expected? Did it improve one thing and make something else worse? Or was the experiment never really testing your idea in the first place?

There’s also a balance between persistence and being willing to give something up. A failed experiment doesn’t necessarily mean the idea is wrong; there might be a bug, or the optimization might be difficult. But you can spend forever rescuing an idea if you don’t ask what evidence would actually make you stop. I try to come back to that: what have we learned, and what’s the next experiment that would distinguish between the explanations we still have?
